claim: Serotonin is implicated in mood and affective disorders.
source: Serotonin (5-HT) is classically known to be implicated in mood and affective disorders (Dayan and Huys, 2009; Cools et al., 2011; Li et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: Serotonin plays a fundamental role when organisms need to adapt to sudden changes in the causal structure of an environment, such as during extinction and reversal learning paradigms.
source: but it also plays a fundamental role when organisms need to adapt to sudden changes in the causal structure of an environment, such as during extinction and reversal learning paradigms (Clarke et al., 2004, 2007; Boulougouris and Robbins, 2010; Bari et al., 2010; Brigman et al., 2010; Berg et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research

claim: 5-HT depletion, particularly in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) of primates, causes perseverative errors.
source: These studies have shown that 5-HT depletion, particularly in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) of primates, causes perseverative errors, that is, difficulties in stopping responses to previously rewarded stimuli which are no longer reinforced, without affecting learning of new associations or retention of learned associations (Clarke et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: 5-HT depletion causes difficulties in stopping responses to previously rewarded stimuli which are no longer reinforced, without affecting learning of new associations or retention of learned associations.
source: These studies have shown that 5-HT depletion, particularly in the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) of primates, causes perseverative errors, that is, difficulties in stopping responses to previously rewarded stimuli which are no longer reinforced, without affecting learning of new associations or retention of learned associations (Clarke et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to prior research

claim: Endogenous 5-HT activation inhibits learned responses that are not currently adaptive.
source: Such results seem to stem from two functions of endogenous 5-HT activation: inhibiting learned responses that are not currently adaptive (Soubrié, 1986; Bari and Robbins, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Endogenous 5-HT activation drives plasticity to reconfigure learned responses.
source: and driving plasticity to reconfigure them (Maya Vetencourt et al., 2008; Jitsuki et al., 2011; He et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Dopamine has dual functions in invigorating reward-related responses and promoting plasticity that reinforces new ones.
source: These mirror dual functions of dopamine (DA) in invigorating reward-related responses (Niv et al., 2007; Panigrahi et al., 2015) and promoting plasticity that reinforces new ones (Tsai et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Steinberg et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DA neurons are activated by reward prediction errors.
source: However, while DA neurons are known to be activated by reward prediction errors (Schultz et al., 1997; Cohen et al., 2012; Eshel et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: The reported firing patterns of 5-HT neurons do not accord with any existing theories.
source: the reported firing patterns of 5-HT neurons (Liu et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016) do not accord with any existing theories (Daw et al., 2002; Boureau and Dayan, 2011; Cools et al., 2011; Nakamura, 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: 5-HT neurons have been proposed to signal worse-than-expected outcomes by being activated by negative reward prediction errors in the reinforcement learning framework.
source: Indeed, 5-HT neurons have been proposed to signal worse-than-expected outcomes by being activated by negative reward prediction errors in the reinforcement learning framework (Daw et al., 2002; Boureau and Dayan, 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: There is little experimental evidence for a negative reward prediction error signal in 5-HT neurons.
source: but there is little experimental evidence for such a signal in 5-HT neurons (Cohen et al., 2015; Hayashi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: 5-HT activation does not appear to drive aversive learning processes.
source: and 5-HT activation does not appear to drive aversive learning processes (Dugué et al., 2014; Liu et al., 2014; McDevitt et al., 2014; Qi et al., 2014; Miyazaki et al., 2014; Fonseca et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: DA drives appetitive learning.
source: the way DA drives appetitive learning (Tsai et al., 2009; Kim et al., 2012; Steinberg et al., 2013)
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research

claim: Pharmacogenetic inactivation of DRN 5-HT neurons slows negative reversal learning.
source: Pharmacogenetic inactivation of DRN 5-HT neurons slows negative reversal learning

claim: Transgenic mice expressing CRE recombinase under the 5-HT transporter promoter (SERT-Cre, n = 8) were transduced with a Cre-dependent adeno-associated (AAV.Flex) virus expressing the synthetic receptor Di (DREADD, hM4D) injected in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN).
source: Transgenic mice expressing CRE recombinase under the 5-HT transporter promoter (Gong et al., 2007) (SERT-Cre, n = 8) were transduced with a Cre-dependent adeno-associated (AAV.Flex) virus expressing the synthetic receptor Di (DREADD, hM4D) (Armbruster et al., 2007) injected in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), the major source of 5-HT to the forebrain (Figure 1A)
evidence: Experimental procedure described in text and shown in Figure 1A

claim: The DRN is the major source of 5-HT to the forebrain.
source: injected in the dorsal raphe nucleus (DRN), the major source of 5-HT to the forebrain (Figure 1A)
evidence: Stated as established knowledge

claim: After training, mice showed learning of the odor–outcome contingencies, as indicated by differences in the anticipatory lick rate.
source: After training, mice showed learning of the odor–outcome contingencies, as indicated by differences in the anticipatory lick rate (Figure 1B bottom)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B

claim: For worse-than-expected outcomes (negative reversals), the kinetics of adaptation to the new contingencies were significantly slower in hM4D mice receiving CNO, compared to hM4D no-CNO controls and WT controls.
source: For worse-than-expected outcomes (negative reversals), the kinetics of adaptation to the new contingencies were significantly slower in hM4D mice receiving CNO, compared to hM4D no-CNO controls and WT controls (Figure 1C,D,E; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B,C)

claim: For better-than-expected outcomes (positive reversals), there was no significant difference between treatment and control groups.
source: In contrast, for better-than-expected outcomes (positive reversals), there was no significant difference between treatment and control groups (Figure 1D,E)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D, E

claim: A population of 5-HT neurons in the DRN contributes to inhibiting perseverative responding.
source: This experiment shows that a population of 5-HT neurons in the DRN contributes to inhibiting perseverative responding, suggesting an anatomical and genetic substrate for previous results obtained with pharmacological and lesion experiments (Clarke et al., 2004, 2007; Boulougouris and Robbins, 2010; Bari et al., 2010; Brigman et al., 2010)
evidence: Inferred from experimental results and supported by citations to prior research

claim: After approximately two weeks of training, mice showed robust CS-triggered anticipatory licking correlated to the reward value of the associated USs (large water > small water > neutral ≈ air puff).
source: After approximately two weeks of training, mice showed robust CS-triggered anticipatory licking correlated to the reward value of the associated USs (large water > small water > neutral ≈ air puff) and eye-blink responses to the delivery of air puffs (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mice showed eye-blink responses to the delivery of air puffs.
source: After approximately two weeks of training, mice showed robust CS-triggered anticipatory licking correlated to the reward value of the associated USs (large water > small water > neutral ≈ air puff) and eye-blink responses to the delivery of air puffs (Figure 2B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B

claim: Mice adapted to reversal of contingencies over 1–3 additional sessions.
source: Anticipatory licking measurements showed that mice adapted to reversal of contingencies over 1–3 additional sessions (Figure 2D)

claim: The specificity of GCaMP6s expression to DRN 5-HT neurons was verified using histological methods.
source: We verified the specificity of GCaMP6s expression to DRN 5-HT neurons using histological methods (Figure 3—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by histological data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Before reversal, photometric 5-HT responses were similar to previous electrical and photometric recordings of identified 5-HT neurons: 5-HT neurons were activated by reward-predicting CSs and air puffs.
source: Before reversal, photometric 5-HT responses were similar to previous electrical (Liu et al., 2014; Cohen et al., 2015) and photometric (Li et al., 2016) recordings of identified 5-HT neurons: 5-HT neurons were activated by reward-predicting CSs and air puffs (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D and supplementary figures, and by citations to prior research

claim: YFP control mice implanted and recorded in the same manner showed no photometric responses to these events.
source: YFP control mice implanted and recorded in the same manner showed no photometric responses to these events (Figure 3—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: DA neurons were activated by reward-predicting cues, and showed small responses to predicted rewards.
source: As expected, DA neurons were activated by reward-predicting cues, and showed small responses to predicted rewards (Figure 3F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F

claim: 5-HT neurons showed little or no response to large water rewards before reversal when they were predicted by the preceding CS, but responded robustly to the same events when they were unpredicted, after reversal.
source: 5-HT neurons showed little or no response to large water rewards before reversal when they were predicted by the preceding CS, but responded robustly to the same events when they were unpredicted, after reversal (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A, B

claim: 5-HT neurons showed an excitatory response to a better-than-expected outcome, or positive reward prediction error (RPE).
source: Thus, 5-HT neurons showed an excitatory response to a better-than-expected outcome, or positive reward prediction error (RPE)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on 5-HT responses to unpredicted rewards

claim: The response to the small reward was also modulated by reward expectation.
source: The response to the small reward was also modulated by reward expectation (Figure 4—figure supplement 1), although to a lesser degree, perhaps due to the presence of a small response even after extensive training (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: DA neurons showed stronger excitatory responses to water rewards immediately after reversal when they violated cue-based predictions, as opposed to before reversal when they occurred as predicted.
source: Like 5-HT neurons, DA neurons also showed stronger excitatory responses to water rewards immediately after reversal when they violated cue-based predictions, as opposed to before reversal when they occurred as predicted (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C

claim: Both 5-HT and DA neurons showed an increase in activity in response to positive RPEs, and both showed a larger response for the larger magnitude RPE.
source: Therefore, both 5-HT and DA neurons showed an increase in activity in response to positive RPEs, and both showed a larger response for the larger magnitude RPE
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on 5-HT and DA responses to unpredicted rewards

claim: Before reversal, the neutral US elicited little response from either 5-HT or DA neurons.
source: Before reversal, this US elicited little response from either 5-HT or DA neurons
evidence: Stated as observation from experimental data

claim: After reversal, the neutral US was presented when a small water reward was predicted, representing a reward omission or negative RPE.
source: After reversal, the neutral US was presented when a small water reward was predicted. Therefore, it represented a reward omission or negative RPE
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design

claim: 5-HT neurons showed a robust excitatory response to the neutral US after reversal.
source: Interestingly, 5-HT neurons showed a robust excitatory response to the neutral US after reversal (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B

claim: DA neurons showed an inhibitory response to the neutral US after reversal.
source: In contrast, DA neurons showed an inhibitory response to the same event (Figure 5C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Midbrain DA neurons respond to positive and negative RPEs with modulation of the opposite sign.
source: Taking the neutral and rewarding USs together, the results show that midbrain DA neurons respond to positive and negative RPEs with modulation of the opposite sign, as reported previously in reward omission paradigms (Cohen et al., 2012; Schultz et al., 1997); but see Matsumoto and Hikosaka (2009); Lammel et al. (2011); Kim et al. (2016); Matsumoto et al., 2016)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data and supported by citations to prior research

claim: SERT-positive DRN 5-HT neurons show excitatory responses to both positive and negative RPEs.
source: On the other hand, SERT-positive DRN 5-HT neurons show excitatory responses to both positive and negative RPEs
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on 5-HT responses to rewards and reward omissions

claim: DRN 5-HT responses to rewards and reward omissions resemble an 'unsigned RPE' or 'surprise' signal.
source: Thus, DRN 5-HT responses to rewards and reward omissions resemble an 'unsigned RPE' or 'surprise' signal (see Discussion)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on 5-HT responses

claim: DRN 5-HT neurons were mildly activated by air puff USs, even after extensive training.
source: In contrast to other USs, DRN 5-HT neurons were mildly activated by air puff USs, even after extensive training (Figure 3; Figure 3—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 3B

claim: Upon reversal, despite the fact that the air puff US now represented a large negative RPE, 5-HT neurons showed no significant response.
source: Upon reversal, despite the fact that the air puff US now represented a large negative RPE (since the large water reward was predicted), 5-HT neurons showed no significant response (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B

claim: Midbrain DA neurons showed no response to the air puff US after training, but showed a small but significant inhibitory response after reversal.
source: Midbrain DA neurons, on the other hand, showed no response to the air puff US after training, but showed a small but significant inhibitory response after reversal (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C

claim: Midbrain DA responses adhered closely to the model of a 'signed RPE', including for the air puff.
source: Overall, midbrain DA responses adhered closely to the model of a 'signed RPE', including for the air puff, whereas the DRN 5-HT neurons resembled an 'unsigned RPE' with respect to rewards and reward omissions, but they diverged from this model for air puff responses (see Discussion for further interpretation)

claim: 5-HT and DA neurons are both sensitive to violations of expectation that occur during an abrupt reversal, with the two systems responding in the same way to better-than-expected outcomes but in opposite ways to worse-than-expected outcomes.
source: Thus, 5-HT and DA neurons are both sensitive to violations of expectation that occur during an abrupt reversal, with the two systems responding in the same way to better-than-expected outcomes but in opposite ways to worse-than-expected outcomes

claim: Water rewards produced larger 5-HT responses when they were presented out-of-context, compared to when preceded by a well-learned cue.
source: We found that water rewards produced larger 5-HT responses when they were presented in this way, compared to when preceded by a well-learned cue (Figure 7B)

claim: Even neutral tones produced an excitatory response when an odor was expected.
source: Of particular interest was that even neutral tones produced an excitatory response when an odor was expected (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1

claim: 5-HT neurons were activated by the substitution of one neutral stimulus with another.
source: Therefore, 5-HT neurons were activated by the substitution of one neutral stimulus with another
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on 5-HT responses to uncued neutral tones

claim: DA neurons responded strongly to uncued rewards, but little to other uncued USs.
source: DA neurons also responded strongly to uncued rewards, as previously reported (Schultz et al., 1997; Cohen et al., 2012), but little to other uncued USs (Figure 7C) (Matsumoto et al., 2016)

claim: With respect to water rewards and reward omissions, 5-HT neurons respond in the same manner to unexpected events, whether negative, neutral or positive, whereas DA neurons are primarily sensitive to unexpected events that have some reward value.
source: Thus, consistent with the responses following CS–US reversal, this experiment also showed that, with respect to water rewards and reward omissions, 5-HT neurons respond in the same manner to unexpected events, whether negative, neutral or positive, whereas DA neurons are primarily sensitive to unexpected events that have some reward value

claim: Before reversal, both 5-HT and DA neurons showed CS responses that correlated with the relative value of the US predicted by the CS (large reward > small reward > neutral ≈ air puff).
source: Before reversal, both 5-HT and DA neurons showed CS responses that correlated with the relative value of the US predicted by the CS (large reward > small reward > neutral ≈ air puff) (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplements 3 and 5)

claim: After the reversal, both 5-HT and DA neurons adjusted to the new contingencies such that, by three days post-reversal, the CS responses reflected their new US associations.

evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8

claim: Despite small differences in their relative magnitudes, and in contrast to their distinct US responses, DA and 5-HT neurons showed CS responses that were remarkably similar, both before and after reversal learning.
source: Thus, despite small differences in their relative magnitudes, and in contrast to their distinct US responses, DA and 5-HT neurons showed CS responses that were remarkably similar, both before and after reversal learning

claim: 5-HT CS responses had a markedly slower rate of adaptation to the new contingencies than did DA CS responses.

claim: The difference in the time constant of CS adaptation was significant for both negative and positive reversals.
source: The difference in the time constant of CS adaptation was significant for both negative and positive reversals, and was not due to differences in learning rates between groups of mice (Figure 9C)

claim: During a positive reversal, because the adaptation of 5-HT cue responses is much slower than that of DA cue responses, the net signal will be transiently biased towards the effects of DA.
source: During a positive reversal, because the adaptation of 5-HT cue responses is much slower than that of DA cue responses, the net signal will be transiently biased towards the effects of DA (Figure 9D, right)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on the difference in learning rates between 5-HT and DA

claim: During a negative reversal, because 5-HT cue responses persist longer than those of DA, the difference will be biased towards the effects of 5-HT.
source: Conversely, during a negative reversal, because 5-HT cue responses persist longer than those of DA, the difference will be biased towards the effects of 5-HT (Figure 9D, left)
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on the difference in learning rates between 5-HT and DA

claim: This suggests a novel mechanism by which 5-HT can contribute to preventing perseverative responding during negative reversals, by directly inhibiting behavioral responses to CSs that have undergone decreases in associated outcome values.
source: This suggests a novel mechanism by which 5-HT can contribute to preventing perseverative responding during negative reversals (Clarke et al., 2007), by directly inhibiting behavioral responses to CSs that have undergone decreases in associated outcome values
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on the difference in learning rates between 5-HT and DA, and supported by citation to prior research

claim: There was a significant correlation between the time constant of DRN 5-HT CS response and the time constant of CS-related licking for the negative reversals but not the positive one.

claim: During negative reversals the time constant of DRN 5-HT responses was slower than that of anticipatory licking for all animals.

claim: 5-HT US responses were strongly sensitive to changes in cue–outcome contingency after the reversal.

claim: 5-HT neurons responded with a similar transient excitation to violations of expectation that were either better-than-expected or worse-than-expected reward outcomes.

claim: Midbrain DA neurons responded oppositely to better-than-expected and worse-than-expected outcomes.

claim: DA neurons could be described as reporting a signed RPE.

claim: 5-HT neurons appeared to report, in part, an unsigned RPE.
source: Thus, whereas DA neurons could be described as reporting a signed RPE, 5-HT neurons appeared to report, in part, an unsigned RPE (but see below for discussion of responses to aversive events)

claim: 5-HT neurons were sensitive not to the direction of error but to its magnitude.

claim: Unsigned prediction error signals have been proposed on theoretical grounds to be ideal for regulating learning and attention based on uncertainty.
source: Unsigned prediction error signals have been proposed on theoretical grounds to be ideal for regulating learning and attention based on uncertainty (Pearce and Hall, 1980; Courville et al., 2006)

claim: By reporting unsigned prediction error signals, 5-HT US responses would be suitable to drive plasticity and re-learning during reversal of contingencies.
source: By reporting such signals, 5-HT US responses would be suitable to drive plasticity and re-learning during reversal of contingencies

claim: The strong excitatory response of the 5-HT system to negative RPEs, caused by reward omissions, provides a possible explanation for why inhibiting this system impairs negative reversal learning.
source: The strong excitatory response of the 5-HT system to negative RPEs, caused by reward omissions, provides a possible explanation for why inhibiting this system impairs negative reversal learning (Clarke et al., 2007; Bari et al., 2010) (Figure 1)

claim: During negative reversals or extinction learning, the 5-HT system, either directly or through an interaction with the DA system, could facilitate trial-by-trial undoing of DA-dependent learning.

claim: Since 5-HT neurons also respond during positive prediction errors, such activation might compete with co-occurring DA signals, slowing positive learning.

claim: The preferential involvement of 5-HT in 'unlearning' responses could be explained by the relative effects of 5-HT release on downstream targets, where 5-HT may favor long-term depression (LTD) and DA long term potentiation (LTP).

claim: Air puff USs continued to evoke responses in 5-HT neurons, even after extensive training, and showed only minor sensitivity to the presence of a predictive cue.

claim: Mice showed air puff–triggered blink responses, but failed to learn anticipatory blinking responses despite extensive training.

claim: 5-HT neurons might report errors of control rather than errors of prediction.

source: Under this hypothesis, an aversive outcome such as the air puff continues to generate a response in 5-HT neurons because the organism has not managed to control this aspect of its environment

claim: Activation of Fos in DRN 5-HT neurons by uncontrollable shocks is lowered by controllability signals from the ventral medial prefrontal cortex.
source: and this activation is lowered by controllability signals from the ventral medial prefrontal cortex (Bland et al., 2003; Amat et al., 2005)

claim: 5-HT CS responses, like DA CS responses, were strongly positively correlated with CS value.

source: Indeed, 5-HT and DA CS signals were qualitatively extremely similar, both after initial training and after relearning
evidence: Inferred from experimental data on 5-HT and DA CS responses

claim: The CS responses of 5-HT neurons were not only much slower than DA neurons to adapt to new associations after the reversal, but were also maintained throughout the extinction of the maladaptive perseverative response.

claim: There was a significant correlation across animals in the post-reversal learning rates of trial-by-trial 5-HT activity and that of anticipatory licking.
source: Furthermore, there was a significant correlation across animals in the post-reversal learning rates of trial-by-trial 5-HT activity and that of anticipatory licking (Figure 10)

claim: The difference in rates of adaptation between DA and 5-HT systems implies that the net balance between DA and 5-HT will undergo specific dynamics during learning that resemble the classical proposal concerning opponent processes by Solomon & Corbit (1974).
